In late 1978, the Rhodesian War was entering its final chapter. Thirteen years earlier, on November 11, 1965, Rhodesia had declared independence, refusing to commit national suicide as the world demanded.

From that day, the country was locked in unending conflict. The early raids against Rhodesia were clumsy failures.

They faded, then returned, stronger and more determined. Despite crushing international sanctions, Rhodesian forces repeatedly outmatched their enemies.

Kill ratios of 10 to 1 were common, with elite units like the light infantry reaching 40 or even 50 to 1.

Yet numbers told a harsher truth. The guerrillas could afford their losses. Rhodesia could not.

Every single soldier mattered. By 1978, Rhodesia was still winning battles, but the pressure from abroad was suffocating.

South Africa, together with Henry Kissinger, forced Prime Minister Ian Smith to accept a path to majority rule.

A transitional government was created with Bishop Muzorewa, Reverend Seathol and Chief Chirao.

The security forces, however, remained under White command. morale at home was faltering, emigration soared and the world closed in on the small nation.

Yet Rhodesia could still fight, and in 1978, its forces would launch their most famous operation.

Rising Terror The year began violently. On January 3rd, terrorists struck the Leopard Rock Hotel.

Within days, civilians near Salisbury were ambushed and murdered, including three brothers aged just 16, 13 and 7.

Their 10-year-old siblings survived only by playing dead. On January 12th, 15-year-old Colin Tilly was shot in the head, outside Salisbury, killed before his father's eyes.

For the first time, terror had reached the capital. The enemy's strategy was simple.

Families filled the cabin. Among them were Hans and Diana Hansen, travelling to visit friends.

Fire tore through the wing. Captain John Hood and First Officer Jeff Beaumont wrestled desperately for control.

Against all odds, they managed a crash landing in a cotton field. The impact was brutal, flames spreading quickly.

Survivors fought to escape through holes in the fuselage. The Hansons helped drag children and wounded hostesses to safety.

Diana, her skirt of flame, ripped it off and carried yet another child to the exit.

Freedom Camp near Lusaka, housing Nkomo's high command. Makushi Camp, sheltering nearly 2,000 cadres, many of them women trained for combat.

According to his system, red or blonde hair signified higher racial status and earned a point.

Hitler, Coca-Cola and the birth of Fanta Adolf Hitler never drank alcohol. But he had a favorite beverage, Coca-Cola.

For years, it was his drink of choice at high-profile Nazi events, served alongside beer and wine.

Across Germany and Austria, civilians and soldiers alike developed a taste for it, buying millions of cases annually.

Within the German military, Coke was second only to beer in popularity. When wartime shortages forced the creation of a new drink, Fanta, Hitler personally endorsed it, helping it become Europe's most successful non-alcoholic beverage during the war.

The story of how that happened begins with a German executive named Max Keith. Coca-Cola in Nazi Germany.

Max Keith, born in Germany but experienced in the American Coca-Cola system, had worked at the company's Atlanta headquarters before being chosen to run Coca-Cola GmbH in Germany in 1933.

That same year, the Nazis rose to power. Keith, then only 30, partnered with American representative Ray Remington Powers to promote Coke aggressively.

They advertised it as the official drink of Nazi Germany. And sales boomed. Coca-Cola became a major sponsor of the 1936 Berlin Olympics, an event that the Nazi leadership saw as an opportunity to project prestige.

Film director Lenny Riefenstahl later explained that Hitler and other officials welcomed sponsors who brought in money.

And Coca-Cola, already established in Germany, was an obvious choice. When Powers died in 1938, Keith took full control of Coca-Cola's German operations.

That same year, sales had exploded. Rising from just 100,000 cases, in 1933 to over 4 million per year by the eve of World War II.

Keith knew the company's reserves would run out by 1942. To protect Coca-Cola GmbH from being seized as enemy property, Keith relied on powerful friends.

The creation of Fanta. With wartime shortages blocking the import of Coca-Cola syrup, Keith looked for a substitute product to keep the factories running.

Their conclusion, the plant should remain in operation, producing a new drink from ingredients available inside Germany.

Keith and Kuhn developed a formula using apple fibre from cider presses, whey from cheese production, beet sugar, and fruit scraps.

Salesman Joe Nipp suggested the name Fanta, short for fantasy. When the first batch was ready in 1941, it sold three million cases in its first year.

Hitler was said to have received the first case himself and approved it. That endorsement ensured increased production and secured Fanta's place as a wartime staple.

The drink was one of the few luxury products exempt from wartime rationing, and high-ranking Nazis ensured its continued production.
